terms.definition: A ghost image you keep seeing after the real picture is gone, usually in the opposite colors, because the cells that looked at it are tired.
One of the three kinds of color-sensing cells in the retina, tuned to long, medium or short wavelengths of light (roughly red, green and blue). Rods, the other type, work mainly in dim light.
The way a sense turns down its response to something steady, so it can notice changes instead. It is why you stop feeling your clothes and why afterimages happen.

The idea that color vision compares signals in opposing pairs: red versus green, blue versus yellow, and light versus dark. Tire one side of a pair and the other side wins, which gives opposite-colored afterimages.
When a nerve cell that is active quiets its neighbors. It sharpens edges, which is why a border between light and dark looks more contrasty than it really is.
Thin bright and dark stripes you see where a smooth gradient meets a flat shade. They are not in the picture. Lateral inhibition is the classic explanation, though it does not explain every detail.
The effect that makes the same gray or the same color look different depending on what surrounds it. A gray square looks lighter on black than on white.
The brain's habit of seeing an object's color as steady while the light changes, by estimating the color of the light and subtracting it.
An assumption your brain makes before looking, such as 'light comes from above' or 'far things are smaller'. Priors make vision fast, and illusions are pictures where a prior gives the wrong answer.

The feeling of motion in a still picture made of repeating dark-to-light steps, strongest in the corner of the eye. Discovered by Fraser and Wilcox in 1979; Kitaoka's rotating snakes are the best-known example.
An edge you see even though no edge is drawn there, because the brain connects separate fragments into a shape in front.
A picture with two equally good interpretations, so the brain flips back and forth between them. The Necker cube and the Rubin vase are examples.
The small difference between what your left and right eyes see. The brain measures it to work out how far away things are.
